title: TSMC posts record Q3 revenue of NT$1.49 trillion, holds earnings call on October 15
subtitle: Reported third-quarter sales of US$46.71 billion rose roughly 50% year on year and beat the top of the company's own US$44.6-45.8 billion guidance, with AI accelerator demand named as the main driver.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: TSMC reported record third-quarter 2026 revenue of NT$1.49 trillion (about US$46.71 billion) in its October 8 pre-announcement, up roughly 50% year on year and above the high end of its own US$44.6-45.8 billion guidance set in July. The chipmaker then held its Q3 earnings call on Thursday, October 15 at 14:00 Taiwan time. Analysts polled by LSEG had going into the call expected net profit of around NT$741-746 billion, which would be a 64-65% year-on-year jump and the company's highest-ever quarterly net income. Revenue leadership for the quarter is attributed to advanced-node demand from Nvidia, Apple, and Broadcom, with 7nm-and-below nodes making up roughly three quarters of wafer revenue in recent quarters.

The AI-attribution story is now mechanical, not narrative. TSMC's July guidance was raised again after it was raised in April; 2026 capex is set at US$60-64 billion, well above the US$52-56 billion range the company gave at the start of the year, and management has said capex over the next three years will be 'significantly higher' than the prior three. The Arizona ramp — US$165 billion already committed, plus another US$100 billion pledged in Q2 — is the explicit answer to the US customer concentration risk that got written into every analyst note after the September Oracle-OpenAI compute reporting.

The pre-call setup also includes a growing supply-side worry. ASML's own Q3 2026 report earlier this week described order books stretching into 2029 and 2030, which is the forward-dated version of TSMC's own guidance behavior; both companies are now visibly booked past the typical two-year semi-cap planning horizon. The question investors wanted answered on the TSMC call was less 'is the quarter good?' — the October 8 revenue number already settled that — and more 'at what point does the capex base-rate have to step up again to match the booked demand?' That is the number that moves the whole AI-infrastructure capex curve by proxy.

For learners: a foundry revenue beat is not the same as a design-house revenue beat. When Nvidia's revenue grows, it is partly margin on existing wafers; when TSMC's revenue grows at this pace, it is almost entirely wafers out the door — which means the physical bottleneck of the entire AI build-out really has moved up a notch, not just the dollar accounting. The reliable way to read these quarters is to triangulate three numbers across the stack: foundry revenue (TSMC), lithography bookings (ASML), and hyperscaler capex (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Oracle). If all three go in the same direction, the industry's capacity story is real; if one lags, that is where the ceiling is.
